text: Bay Ganyo, after finally convincing himself that there was no possibility of lodging with Yirechek, picked up his saddlebags, without heeding the host’s entreaties to leave them at his house until he found accommodation, and set off, accompanied by the servant, for Nàrodny Kavàrna — the café where Bulgarian students gathered. It was already seven o’clock when he entered the café with the saddlebags in his hand and the kalpak on his head. Go on, try not to recognize who he is and where he is from! To the left of the entrance, around a table, were sitting several Bulgarian students.

One of them saw the incoming compatriot and nudged the others: “Bulgarian, Bulgarian!” Everyone turned at the moment when Bay Ganyo stopped a waiter carrying a tray of coffees and, trying as much as possible to distort the Bulgarian words so as to make them understandable to the foreigner, asked in a loud voice: “Where here Bulgarian boys?” — and accompanied the question with a movement of his head and his free hand. A burst of laughter from the left side put an end to the waiter’s perplexity. Bay Ganyo turned and recognized his black-eyed, black-haired, huddled compatriots.

— Oh! Good day! Have you been here? — he cried heartily, set down the saddlebags, and began to seize the students’ hands. — Why are you looking at me? Don’t be afraid, I’m Bulgarian... Make room for me to sit down.
— What is your name, sir? — one of the students inquired curiously.
— Me? Why do you ask? Ganyo Balkanski. I brought a little rose oil to your Prague — here it is in the saddlebags.
“Is that so?” cried one of the younger students in patriotic ecstasy. “Come on, let us see it.”
He had indeed only heard of rose oil.
— What are you going to look at in it, oil is oil — replied Bay Ganyo — it’s not for you. Leave the oil alone and tell me something else: where am I to settle down? I was just now at Mr. Irechek’s...
“Is that so?” cried the exalted student again.

— “How so?” Why shouldn’t I go to him? I went — I thought he’d show some human decency, invite me to his home as a guest. Such faith! “My place is too cramped,” he says, “and I don’t know what else, I don’t know what.” He loves, he says, Bulgarians... Him! When there’s profit to be had, your Uncle Ganyo knows how to love too. — Is that how you welcome a Bulgarian? A Bulgarian!... Not to lie to you, the man fed me. And what a meal — well, let’s just say, it was enough to choke on!... Where are Bulgarians more hospitable; a Bulgarian, even if he has only one room, will still invite you...

Some of the students began to realize where Bay Ganyo was heading and were waiting from one minute to the next for him to show his hand. Only the exalted student responded sympathetically to his words and openly shared his indignation at the foreigners’ lack of hospitality.
— Indeed, our Bulgarians are very hospitable — he confirmed with the greatest confidence, — the locals don’t want to know you. We’re just hanging around here in the cafés...

The student who uttered those words was very advanced in civilization, but for some reason he did not enjoy any particular reputation among his comrades; it seemed that certain sins weighed on his soul; among other things, people said that he was very fond of “making a quick profit.” No wonder! That cursed sin—miserliness—through the contagion of the surrounding domestic environment takes root almost from childhood; it dries up the soul of the young man, turning him into the coldest of egoists: nothing tender, nothing noble remains in him. Material interest governs all the miser’s actions and determines his relations with those around him: no moral impulse precedes, no remorse follows his actions, directed without regard for the means toward the obtaining of advantages. Even when those actions bring disaster or shame to someone, even then, instead of pangs of conscience, the selfish miser feels satisfaction, as if others’ loss were his gain, others’ misfortune his happiness. Only one thing would disturb our young egoist—to be outwitted by someone. When in other nations the word “clever” is synonymous with cunning, treacherous, and, when attached to a person, would lower him in society’s esteem, among us the epithet clever is worn like the most honorable decoration: “Well! What a clever boy he turned out to be, may his father live long, he fooled us all! We couldn’t deceive him! Bravo. Well done!”

No actions or relationships had any meaning for Bodkov — that was his name — unless something tangible, some profit, came out of them. (Are there words in the European languages corresponding to these, in this sense?) If he visited the local families, he did not do so out of sociability, or from a desire to become acquainted with the way of life in more civilized circles; the intellectual and moral interests of that society not only did not engage him, but were a burden to him — they seemed like boring intervals, unbearable pauses, separating him from the aim of his visits — from the tangible: some little feast, or some outing at their expense. He could not imagine acquaintance with women without ulterior motives. He kept a whole list of girls — how much dowry each had; nothing else interested him in that respect. Interest likewise determined his relations with his comrades. Flattery, slander, intrigues, and denunciations were the instruments of his advantage. Even things like national and tribal sympathies and antipathies served him only to extract personal gain. More than once he had dipped his hand into the purses of various Slavic committees, now as “from Batak,” now as an “emigrant.” But Aslanov is more of a master at such things.

Such was the exalted student, who supported Bay Ganyo in his opinion about the ego-hospitality of foreigners. — Yes, we linger here about the cafés; nobody invites us to visit — he repeated, to please Bay Ganyo.

— Well then, why do you want them to let you loaf around? — said a student with a bitter expression, who, it seemed, had long been harboring hatred toward the young egoist, with a contemptuous smile. — Do you want to be carried on their hands? Why? Because, not yet having managed to cross the threshold of their house, you will first flirt with the maid who meets you in the corridor? Because in their society you either keep silent like an oak, or open your mouth only to babble vulgarities and nonsense? Because to their faces you will praise them to the skies, and behind their backs you will slander them? Because you will throw dust in their eyes and present yourself as the son of a millionaire manufacturer or a shipowner, when your father has two spindles for braid-making or two broken crows — just so you can bewitch the parents and carry off their daughter? Why should they receive you with open arms? Who are you? What are you to them? Whom do you impress with your hospitality? And what is this vaunted hospitality of yours! — Is it that the Bulgarian will spread a greasy mattress for you and cover you with a dubious blanket? Ah, for God’s sake, enough of these savage boasts! Isn’t it time we opened our eyes already?
— What are you getting worked up about, man? Did you just now find the time to argue? — one of the students chimed in, — when we have a guest?

— Let the man have his say a little, he doesn’t want money, does he? — Bay Ganyo reassured him with this typical argument: “H e   d o e s n ’ t   w a n t   m o n e y !” He may say whatever he likes, do whatever he likes, so long as he doesn’t ask for money, so long as he doesn’t touch our pocket, our interests. He may even lie, he doesn’t want money!

But after this accidental incident, no friendly conversation could be maintained anymore. The company fell silent, and one after another they began to leave. Of the Bulgarians, only Bay Ganyo and the exalted student remained, who did not want to miss the chance to derive some benefit from his chance encounter with the Bulgarian rose-oil merchant. — The pot rolled until it found its lid.

Not an hour had passed, and the student had managed so thoroughly to blacken his comrades before Bay Ganyo that he made him exclaim with all his heart: “Ashkolsun, kyopeoolar!”

An hour later Bay Ganyo was already in the student’s room, and the student knew quite skillfully how to exploit to his own advantage the arrival of the guest, whom he introduced to his landlords as his relative, a millionaire who “has a whole lot of rose-oil factories.” He managed to borrow from the landlady—whom he had not paid rent for the room in quite a long time—ten guilders.

While in one room the student was extolling Bay Ganyo’s wealth, in the neighboring room Bay Ganyo had already taken off his anteria and was searching in it for something with great attention, muttering under his breath: “That damned vermin has shown up again.”

The notion of cleanliness is not developed to a very high degree in Bay Ganyo. “Can a living person be without vermin?” say the old people among us, and, reassured by this axiom, they do not very zealously hinder the multiplication of the little creatures. And why should they deprive themselves of such a pleasure: the sun is shining hot—what use is that sun if one cannot go out onto the porch, stretch out on the mat, sneeze two or three times from its dust, then have grandmother come, put his head on her knee, and she stick her bony fingers with mourning nails into his hair and, as if she were shelling rice, begin to pick! — here, pick! — there, and when the little creatures get frightened, and start to crawl over the head, then a pleasant tickling, and then grandmother begins to sing, and that Balkan sun is blazing hot! Idyl...

Bay Ganyo, after he had finished his entomological investigations, straightened up his attire and, without knocking, entered the neighboring room, but immediately cried: “Pardon!” — and he had reason to: he found himself in a very tender vis-à-vis between the student and the landlady’s daughter — they had embraced, as befits two young loving hearts. The girl, ashamed, ran into the other room.
— Hey, why are you coming in like that? You’re embarrassing the girl — said the student with an ironic wink.
— You’ve hit the jackpot! — whispered Bay Ganyo mysteriously, his eyes shining like those of a monastery tomcat. — Shiny, the devil take it! Is she a maid?
— What a maid! The landlady’s daughter!

— Is that so? Here you can’t tell who is the maid and who is the mistress; they’re all shiny, all neatly dressed. One of them steps out in front of you, smiling so sweetly and ingratiatingly—you think she’s a maid, you tease her, and you bring trouble on your head; another one steps out, pretty and modest—you think, ah, this must be the mistress, you stand up for her, invite her to sit down, she’s shy—damn it!—you speak to her politely, and then you see her cleaning your boots!

From the student’s stories, accompanied by various gestures with which he embellished and gave greater force and meaning to his words, Bay Ganyo learned that for several months the young man, under the guise of pure love, had been attacking the widow landlady’s daughter with irresistible persistence.

— And she, the wild one — explains the narrator, — hopes that I’ll take her for a wife! Let her hope, and let her feed me nicely, let her sew me shirts. If she were some rich woman — I’d understand a man taking her, but she’s a pauper like me. She’s winding herself around me because she thinks I’m a rich man. If she knew what I really am, would she still be after me? The local women are terrible speculators! But I know how to handle them too, don’t I? — And he went on at length about how he handles them...
— Bravo! — cried Bay Ganyo with oily eyes, delighted by the young interlocutor.

— Wait a minute, is that all? If that’s all, then forget it! There’s another one, another one—I’ve got my eye on her, but who knows! If only I could turn her head—there’s something worth going after. Rich! I’m invited to their place tomorrow as a guest, and they’re going to take me to a village for a walk.
— Well, when will you take me to the factories? — asked the practical Bay Ganyo.

— Easy work, the day after tomorrow. You stay here tomorrow, hang around them; when they see that you don’t know the language, they won’t let you go to the inn, they’ll invite you to their place, and you’ll get a free meal.

And indeed, the next morning early the student went out visiting, and Bay Ganyo remained in the lodging alone with the landlords. As usual, that day too he got up very early, woke and sent off his companion, and waited yet another whole hour until the hostesses should wake up. This waiting was very hard for him; he felt some great need, like any person, and he had forgotten to ask the student where that thing was, and—whether he wanted to or not—he had to wait for the household to get up and, shame or no shame, ask them. It is very bad when a person does not know the language abroad; for the simplest thing they cannot understand you, you always have to explain with your hands, with your fingers, show them... But can every thing be shown? Bay Ganyo knew languages: he could talk to you in Turkish like a Turk, he understood Vlach, Serbian, Russian a little here and there, but the Germans and the Czechs do not understand any of those languages. It cannot be said that Bay Ganyo did not know German at all; he knew one word and another.

In the neighboring room the ladies got up and began to bustle about. Bay Ganyo looked through the keyhole, not out of any indecent curiosity, but to see whether they were already dressed and, carefully, holding his breath, as he made himself acquainted with their toilette, he composed in his mind a phrase in German that would correspond to our: “Where is that, for a big job?” — and at last, from the literal translation, he cobbled together the phrase: “Wo is diese fur gross Arbeit?” — Knock! knock! knock!
— Please! — two female voices called from the neighboring room.
Bay Ganyo opened the door, said a “pardon,” and shyly uttered: — Wo is diese fur gross Arbeit? — and gestured with his fingers to emphasize the question.
— What, sir? — asked the girl in bewilderment, trying to examine the appearance of the millionaire recommended by her lover.
— For gross work? — repeated Bay Ganyo, even more embarrassed, and again gestured with his fingers and with his head, but he noticed that they had not understood him.
They understood him, but not as they should have; the women thought that he was telling them that he had come to do big business, a large trade in rose oil.

„Hey, the devil! — thinks Bay Ganyo. — What am I to do now?“ — And so that at least the daughter would not be a witness to his awkward predicament, he beckoned the mother into his room with his hand, closed the door, and after repeating the question again in German, this time added it with a desperate mime, which made the lady flee, choking with suppressed laughter, into the other room. The maid appeared and satisfied Bay Ganyo’s curiosity. A trio of uninterrupted female laughter shook the walls.

The aroma coming through the open kitchen door into the corridor whetted Bay Ganya’s appetite, and out of curiosity he peeped in to see what they were cooking. There were the mistress of the house and the maid.

— What is that? — asked Bay Ganyo in a condescending tone, not so much out of a desire to get acquainted with the culinary art of the Czechs, as to show that he had been around Europe and knew such things, and that he also knew how to speak German. — Soup, right? You’re making soup? I know. Ich versten supa!

And Bay Ganyo, with a mixture of German, Bulgarian, and mangled Bulgarian, aided by impressive gesticulations, made the landlady understand that he would not refuse to taste the flavor of their cuisine. When he saw that the women showed a greater inclination to explain themselves in Czech, Bay Ganyo also switched to “Czech” and reinforced his condescending wish with the words: “ya khocham kushay,” which he interpreted by repeatedly touching his fingers to his open mouth, and then, pointing to his three fingers, he jabbed his chest with his index finger, jabbed the same finger toward the landlady’s chest, and a third time pointed into space, as if indicating the landlady’s invisible daughter, that is, “to eat together, the three of us!” For Bay Ganyo it was also important to know at what hour he would have lunch, since he intended to go for a walk, so as not to miss lunch, and then “give money for food, while there is free food, for nothing,” and therefore he took out his huge watch and, holding it up in front of the landlady’s nose, made her point with her finger at the hands to show him when he would “kushay.” When he was convinced that everything was in order, Bay Ganyo went into his room, stuffed the little rose-oil flasks into his belt, and went out into the street for a walk, and at the same time he would take a walk and perhaps run into some customer for rose oil.

He looked around, and seeing that many streets intersected, that one could easily take the wrong road and get lost, the practical man glanced about to notice some sign by which he might recognize the house, and he saw on the opposite side, on a back wall, an inscription in large letters; he took out his notebook, moistened his thumb, copied down the inscription exactly, and, fully convinced that he had in his hands the most precise address of his lodging, he plunged into the narrow streets of old Prague, now glancing at this, now at that, now here a shop, now there a shop, got carried away, and not only got carried away, but lost his way completely. And now what? Why, when he set out to look for his house, he got even more tangled up in the Jewish streets, and an hour passed, then two hours passed; he would run into some house—there was no way out; he would take another direction, walk and walk, and suddenly emerge on the bank of the Vltava. “Well, devil take it, now what?” And never mind the rest, but lunchtime came, came and went. That old Bay Ganyo trudged on and on, walking and walking, drenched to the skin, out of breath, looking like anything but himself. The people he met, especially the policemen, looked at him suspiciously, which only confused him further. “Well, devil take it, now what?” And he was hungry too, there was a revolution in his stomach, but why the devil should he throw his money to the wind when he had been invited to lunch?

But, you may ask, why does Bay Ganyo wander about the streets when the address is in his pocket? Well, that’s the point! Bay Ganyo is no fool; do you think he did not think of taking out his little notebook, stopping one person or another in the street, and, showing him the written address, asking him with his finger “which way”? He knows these things; he stops both men and women, but here is the strange thing — whoever he stops and asks, as soon as he shows the written address, either looks at him in astonishment and laughs, or turns away from him in indignation. One lady, probably some nervous old maid, when he showed her the address, snapped at him so sharply that even Bay Ganyo lost heart. “Well, damn it, either I’m crazy, or all Prague has gone mad,” he thinks to himself, and cannot stop wondering at the effect produced by his written address; while thinking, he keeps looking around, and then all at once — can you believe his luck? — he sees in front of him the Nàrodny Kavàrna, the café where Bulgarian students gather. Bay Ganyo goes inside and finds the angry student.
— Good day! Well, tell me, your grace, am I the crazy one, or are the people here crazy? — asks Bay Ganyo, out of breath, with wet hair stuck to his forehead.
The student looked at him questioningly. Bay Ganyo told him how he had gotten lost, how he had inquired about his house by address, and what they had answered him.
The student, knowing that the Czechs, rough and fanatical only toward the Germans, are otherwise quite courteous, cannot help wondering how they could fail to do a favor for Bay Ganyo.
— Please, read what it says here! — and Bay Ganyo handed over the little notebook.
The student read it: at first he frowned a little, then burst out laughing!...
— Did you show this address to any lady? — he asked with a laugh.
— Why? I showed it, you know! Eh?
— Well? Do you know what is written here?
— What?
— It is written “...Zde je zapovedeno...” “Here it is forbidden to...” You copied it from some wall.
— Indeed! Look! T... t... t! Are you telling the truth? Look! — said Bay Ganyo, clicked his tongue a little, and then he too began to laugh.

The student did not know Bodkova’s apartment; they did not visit one another, and so he advised Bay Ganyo to wait, since some Bulgarian would surely come along and point out the house to him. It is easy to say “wait,” but let us see whether Bay Ganyo’s stomach was of the same opinion! And that it was not of the same opinion, he proved it demonstratively with an endless growling.
— Are you not hungry? — the student asked him, hearing the revolutionary signals.

— Me? — I’m not — lied old Gancho a little, because if he told the truth, the other man would show him the inn, and he certainly did not want to admit to him (“How am I supposed to tell such a stubborn brat!”) that a good meal was waiting for him at the hosts’ place.

A conversation between Bay Ganyo and the “contrary little brat” could not get started. From the very first meeting, and instinctively somehow, they sensed that they were not made for each other, because, according to the Bulgarian proverb (ah, what exquisite proverbs the Bulgarian genius has created!) “mangy donkeys smell each other from nine hills away.” One had come from Bulgaria, the other had lived in Europe; surely they would have had something to talk about, since after all there must be some difference between the West and our fatherland. However, Bay Ganyo did not sense this difference, and how could he! Wherever he went, he carried his own atmosphere, his own customs and habits with him; he looked for lodging according to his own tastes, met only his own kind of people, to whom he was accustomed and in whom, of course, he saw nothing new: if he went to Vienna, he would stop at the “London” hotel, where it was just as stuffy, and smelled just as much of kitchen fumes and hydrogen sulfide as at home; he met the same Turks, Armenians, Serbs, and Arnauts that he was used to seeing every day; he would not go to the “Habsburg” café, because he was afraid of being fleeced, but would again enter the Greek café, which was just as dirty and stifling with perpetual smoke as our cafés are. If he went on business, he would go to the Bulgarian merchants, and through them he would not even realize that he was coming into contact with Europeans. And that it is precisely outside this limited sphere that European life begins, he neither knows nor, it seems, even wants to know. The education, the moral world of the European, his domestic surroundings — the fruit of centuries of tradition and gradual refinement, the intellectual movement, social struggles and the way they are conducted, museums, libraries, philanthropic institutions, the fine arts, the thousands of manifestations of progress — none of this burdens Bay Ganyo’s attention.

“Because my father always listened to operas,” says Bay Ganyo, and, enchanted by this principle of petrification and ultra-retrogression, he is not too alarmed by the “new fashion,” that is, by civilization. But despite all this, Bay Ganyo does not have the courage of the Chinese—to wall himself off with a wall against the invasion of civilization—and although he is inspired by the principle “my father did not do this, and I will not do it either,” you suddenly see that you have put on a clean shirt, put on gloves, and when they press him, he puts on a frock coat too; he gets angry, he laughs, but he puts on the frock coat. You hear him say “pardon,” talk about the “constitution,” boast here and there that he likes “soup,” when in fact he would prefer a spicy stew to all European dishes.
— Ah, here comes a little Bulgarian boy; he knows Bodkova’s lodgings — declared the “stubborn little brat”...

— Come, lead me home — said Bay Ganyo to the little Bulgarian in such a tone that it ought to disappear even from our dealings with lazy servants; but the words “politeness,” “courtesy” are newly borrowed from the Russian language, “delicacy” is borrowed from the French, and among us the most suitable term for these notions is the word “syrupy sentimentality.” These soft, gentle, heartfelt forms of address, which characterize the relations of civilized people and make life kinder, more pleasant, are incomprehensible to Bay Ganyo; he speaks as God gave him speech: “Come on, hey, listen, take me home.” And what does this mean: “I beg you, have the kindness, be so kind,” what is all this syrupy sentimentality!...

The little Bulgarian boy led Bay Ganyo to the gate of his lodging and went back. Bay Ganyo looked at the miserable inscription on the opposite wall, shook his head at it, clicked his tongue, and went into the house. In the corridor he met no one; he peeped into the kitchen — there the fire had already gone out, the dishes were cleaned and put away. “Tsk, what a pity, I missed the profit,” muttered Bay Ganyo, went into his room, squatted over his saddlebags, took the little flasks out from his belt and stuffed them inside, pulled out the greasy kashkaval, cut himself a piece of dry bread, and began to stifle the revolution, smacking his lips so appetizingly that even the laziest Swiss cow would have envied him. To irritate his lymphatic organs, weary from unproductive labor, he let down his gullet a chewed Arnaut pepper, which made him burst into tears and accompany his smacking with sniffling. The maid, who was bustling about in the adjoining room, hearing the strange sounds with which Bay Ganyo accompanied his breakfast, opened the door and peeped into the room: Bay Ganyo shyly hid the saddlebags behind his back, turned his tearful and sweaty face, said “pardon!”, sniffed energetically through his nose, and drove the maid away, that is, not that he told her to go out, but she hastened to run away, thinking that the millionaire might have received some sad news.

Bodkov did not return in the evening. Toward dusk the ladies came back; a fire was lit again in the kitchen and they began to prepare supper. Bay Ganyo already considers himself familiar, “and after all, with women what’s there to stand on ceremony for” — says he, and without any preamble enters the kitchen and explains, more with gestures than with words, that he had lost his way in the streets and missed lunch, but no matter — he still has one lunch coming to him, he will make it up with a supper. Bay Ganyo also understands culinary art, and not only does he understand it, but any violation of that craft enrages him. He saw, for example, that the hostess was about to put a fresh fish into the boiling water, and he rose with all his energy, seized the hostess’s hand, pulled the fish out with the other hand, and made a sign with his hand and head, meaning: “Stop, don’t move, just watch how fish is cooked!” “Salt!” — commands Bay Ganyo. They give him salt; he rolls up his sleeves to the elbows on his hairy arms, plunges his not-so-delicate fingers into the saltcellar, and begins to salt and rub the already salted fish outside and inside. “Red pepper!” — but where would those savages have red pepper! “Black pepper” — commands Bay Ganyo, grabs the pepper, and rubs it over the fish. “Grill!” — trumpets the triumphant cook, but here they could not understand him, despite all his gestures, and he himself looked around and could not spot a grill; but is that an obstacle for Bay Ganyo? He is no yesterday’s man! Taking the tongs, he raked all the fire toward the opening of the oven, left the other dishes to rest (it was well that they were already ready), spread the tongs apart, placed the fish on them, and tried to slide it into the oven, but the little door was narrow; the fish caught, slipped, and — splash! — into the fire. “Ah!” — cried the hostess. “Nothing, nothing!” — Bay Ganyo reassured her, grabbed the fish, blew off the stuck-on coals and ash, and put it back on the grill. Smoke and the smell of fish filled the whole kitchen. The ladies — in despair, Bay Ganyo — radiant; he is now in his element; he is grilling the fish and blowing and sniffing, irritated by the appetizing smoke, while with his free hand, smeared from turning the fish, he commands them to set the table so that his dish won’t get cold: “Fresh fish isn’t hot — throw it away!” The fish, baked, with its tail and head rolled in ash, was placed on a plate and, under Bay Ganyo’s courteous command: “Quick! Quick! While it’s hot, bring lemon and wine; without wine it isn’t worth two pennies!” — they sat down around the table, sending the maid running for lemon and wine. What could they do! The millionaire was not going to change his habits for their pleasure, was he! The hostess reached out to cut the fish. “Please, please, please! For heaven’s sake!” — cried Bay Ganyo and held her hand, then turned the fish over onto its back, pressed here and there with his two fingers, and it split into two halves. Well, go on and don’t rejoice! The maid brought the lemon; Bay Ganyo cut it, took half in a whole handful, and squeezed it over the plate with such care that even the fleshy parts of the lemon fell onto the fish. What do you think, doesn’t Bay Ganyo have an appetite? Hardly as much lemon juice flowed into the plate as saliva Bay Ganyo swallowed. And wine was brought too. Supper began.

Carlsbad and I don’t know what other “-bad” they recommend the Aesculapiuses to those suffering from catarrh of the stomach. Let those sufferers be taken by the ear and placed at the table before Bay Ganyo, and then let their stomachs be upset even more than the streets of Yuchbunar... you will see what effect the spectacle will have on them!... Bay Ganyo eats, oh yes, he is no joke, he eats till his ears flap! All the organs of his body are in motion, and first of all his teeth, tongue, and nose. Here one realizes the poverty and inadequacy of language! With what words, with what interjections, with what punctuation marks, and finally with what musical notes is it possible to depict those smacking, grunting, snuffling, clattering, clicking, sucking sounds that pour from Bay Ganyo like hail!... Blessed are the hostesses! Not every Czech woman will have the good fortune to enjoy such a spectacle.

They had finally eaten. They went into the reception room. Bay Ganyo, red as a peony, kept twisting his little mustache, kept belching into his hand, and kept muttering “pardon.” They settled into the chairs. Bay Ganyo rolled a cigarette, greasy from his fingers, and began to suck on it and blow clouds of smoke through his mustache. Is this not the most fitting moment for enjoyment: for music, for songs, for love? The girl caught the mood of the millionaire and asked him whether he liked music. Who? Bay Ganyo? Why, if Bay Ganyo does not like music, who else would like it? Who else has been able to inspire the gypsies, that is, the musicians, with such respect for himself as Bay Ganyo? Just let him wink at them, and look what happens to those gypsies! Fire! Fire! Twist that violin of yours, make that clarinet squeal!
Your body is like a poplar tree,
to my heart like two stakes.
On your dress, I’m pulling.
burn my liver...

— Sus 6e, chengene! Ne shcha az lyubovni! Na rakia mi sviri! — cried Bay Ganyo to them and clinked his glass on the table. They start “Karan-karanfiltcheto,” Bay Ganyo clinks his glass, they stop. They start “Ne shtemi niy bogatstvo” — again he clinks his glass. They turn to “Zelen listec.” “Ha, vidyakhte li sega! E-e-e-e-h! Gel kefim, gel!”... — and bang the bottle on the ground or in the window... Well, who is the master of such things? And was it only once, or twice? But t h e s e   w o m e n   how would they know who your uncle Ganyo is! And even if you tell them how many panes you’ve broken with music, they can’t understand!...

— I love music! — said Bay Ganyo condescendingly. — I love music! — he repeated and shook his head, which in his opinion expressed the sad necessity of having to listen, for the women’s sake, to some miserable tinkling on the piano. “What do you understand about playing, about conversation?” Bay Ganyo thought to himself.

The girl opened the piano and began a series of endless pieces from Smetana’s *The Bartered Bride*. Under her fingers there poured forth the sounds that bring every Czech soul to ecstasy. Her mother, who was probably hearing those pieces for the thousand and first time, was steeped in bliss, and in her gaze, turned toward Bay Ganyo, national pride and self-satisfaction shone; she kept her head in time with the tempo of the piece, now adagio, now allegro, as though punctuating the notes of the flourishes with her nose. From time to time she signaled to Bay Ganyo with her eyes, warning him of the approach of some favorite moment in the piece, and the millionaire would answer: “Be careful, your grace, don’t look at me, I’ve heard them how many times for s u c h   t h i n g s!...” And in order to back up this sign of his with deeds, he got up from the chair precisely at the moment when the hostess expected to enjoy the effect Smetana would produce on Bay Ganyo, and hurriedly, with a plan in his head, went to his room, took from his saddlebags the muskal opened for trial, and returned to the reception room, winked at the mother: “watch what will have an effect,” tiptoed up to the girl, carried away by the music, and — that Bay Ganyo was a terrible devil! — opened the muskal with rose oil and gently shoved it under the girl’s nose. She, upon feeling the breath of Bay Ganyo’s sweaty hand, stinking of fish, turned away in disgust and, still absorbed in the music, at first looked at him with a frown, but instantly came to herself, realizing that the millionaire stood before her and was grinning at her, asking: “Does your Smetana suit you better, or this thing you smelled, eh?” — and he tucked the muskal into his belt... The girl stopped playing. Bay Ganyo began... (What did you say? — I couldn’t understand you!)... He began to play carelessly with one finger, without sitting down on the chair: “Just enough to let these people know that we too understand a little about these doohickeys.” One of Bay Ganyo’s relatives had come into possession of a hand accordion with keys, so now and then, when he was in the mood, Bay Ganyo would break his fingers trying to pick out some song. Now he began a startled pizzicato, which in his opinion rendered the song: “Stole la” say, granny’s, sla-slanin-kaaa, bacon, stole granny’s bacon...” the whole of “Bacon” being stolen from the Czech “Slaninka.”
— Pan is playing “Slaninka,” mama! — the girl announced her discovery.
— “Slaninka,” sir — said Bay Ganyo, — how do you know it?

Delighted by his success, Bay Ganyo sat down on the chair to play, now quite seriously, something more substantial. And what could be more substantial than “The Night Is Terrible”? Bay Ganyo began to p l a y, but he himself remained dissatisfied with the performance. And quite naturally! “The Night Is Terrible” was not created for the piano; the sounds interfere with one another: you press the key for “terr-i-i-ible!” and the voice gets cut off; the harmonica is another matter! Once you put your finger on “... terr-i-i-ible...” — press away, damn it! Let it drone for half an hour, press, bend it in waves, until you feel like it! But with the piano — plink, plink, nothing! Bay Ganyo saw that the effect produced by “The Little Bacon” would weaken, thought and thought, and then decided: “Well, wait, let me sing ‘The Night Is Terrible’ to these women!...” He pondered a bit, wanted to tune himself to a mournful mood, in the spirit of the plaintive song, sighed deeply once, put his right hand to his ear, half-closed his eyes, and when he opened his mouth!...

„Grandissimo maestro Verdi! You have no enemies, you cannot have enemies! But if, against all expectation, some monster should appear, he will be the devil himself. God is great, Esimio Maestro! — and all the arrows of the evil spirit are powerless against you! Only one thing... only one means can the cunning one employ, and the whole musical world will be covered in mourning... We shall pray, and you too pray, Divin Maestro, to the almighty Creator, not to allow Satan to lead you into the hall where Bay Ganyo is singing “Night is terrible”... And when your most delicate hearing is shaken by the wild, inhuman sounds incomprehensible to you, may the Evil Spirit reveal the terrible truth to you with his satanic laughter: Ha! ha! ha! Verdi! This is a song from your   d i v i n e   “Traviata”! Ha! ha! ha! ha-a!!...“
— It’s already late, gentlemen — said the shy Ilcho, glancing at his watch, — midnight! Let’s go home, and another time, God willing, we’ll talk again about Bay Ganyo.

— Hey, Ilcho, tell me, why do you hate Bulgarian songs so much? — Dravichkata asked as they were leaving. — Who? Me, hate them? Sorry, my dear, you’ve misunderstood me badly. I am capable of admiring, of losing myself, of being carried away to ecstasy by our beautiful melancholic folk songs, but by Bulgarian songs, not by those disgusting parodies of foreign vulgar songs that our Bay Ganyo types hand down to us, twisted beyond recognition through those Gypsy appoggiaturas and throat-wrenching with drunken trills and flourishes... We have songs, but we have no singers. I am ready to embrace my enemy if he sings to me properly the song “Bogdane, may God strike you dead” or “Come on, Velo girl, roll up your white sleeves,” and to look askance at my friend when I see him admiring “Green Little Leaf,” “The Little Carnation,” and other such Gypsy delights...
